added: The church of St Dochdwy lies on an important early Christian site and a pre-Norman conquest cross shaft (NPRN 301373) is located to the south-west of the church.

The present church was built by David Jones of Penarth to the design of Bristol architect Samuel Charles Fripp and was consecrated in 1866. It comprises a chancel, South tower, aisled nave, and North vestry. The exterior has snecked rubble facings with slate roofs and freestone dressings. There is a 5-light traceried window to the West front. Internally the nave has 3-bay pointed-arch arcades and

[Additional:] The church was rebuilt twice in the C19th. (1) section 38(4)(a) of the Limitation Act defines adverse possession as possession ‘in whose favour the limitation can run’. This phrase is directed not to the nature of the possession, but to the capacity of the squatter: JA Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham [2003] 1 AC 419; [2002] UKHL 30 at [35] per Lord Browne-Wilkinson, who gave as an example of a person not in adverse possession and in whose favour

(3) the possession must be peaceful and not have been acquired by force (nec vi), be open and not stealthy (nec clam) and not be by consent of the true owner (nec precario). These requirements were articulated by Bryson J in Beever v Spaceline Engineering Pty Ltd (1993) 6 BPR 13,270 as ‘actual, open, visible, notorious, continuous and hostile to the title of the true owner’.

See: Hughes v Griffin [1969] 1 WLR 23; Mulcahy v Curramore Pty Ltd [1974] 2 NSWLR 464; Powell v McFarlane (1979) 38 P & Cr 452; BP Properties v Buckler (1987) 55 P & Cr 337; National Australia Bank Ltd vGolden Sea Dragon (Hobart) Pty Ltd (1992) 4 Tas R 250; Lee v Ferno Holdings Pty Ltd (1993) 33 NSWLR 404; Shaw v Garbutt (1996) 7 BPR 14,816; Cooke v Dunn (1998) 9 BPR 16,489; JA Pye (Oxford) Ltd v
Section 38 of the Limitation Act 1969 (NSW) outlines how the limitation period for recovering land is affected by adverse possession:
Ownership and Estrangement : In 1999, the plaintiff inherited 5 and 7 xxxx Street, and her brother inherited nearby properties. They became estranged and had no contact for many years.

Plaintiff’s Situation : The plaintiff was said to reside at No 55, but the property appeared derelict. Until 2000, the plaintiff had a tenant at No. Five, following which the managing agent (CobdenHayson) maintained the property and paid rates until 2014.

Defendant’s Entry: In 2009, the defendant learned from her brother about three abandoned properties, including Nos 5, 7, and 55. She inspected them and believed No. 5 was unoccupied. She began visiting and cleaning No. 5 monthly, storing items and making basic repairs.

Occupation and Use : The defendant moved to Sydney in 2011, stored furniture at No 5, and claimed to use it as a base. In 2012, she and her daughter Chantal began using No 7 following the tenant’s departure. Chantal claimed she later resided at both properties part-time and then full-time.

Great House Farmhouse and barn formed an attractive group, built of local lias
limestone, and occupied an historic site next to the parish church. Finds of
medieval ironwork and pottery have been reported from the site. Great House was
the chief freehold farm of the parish and was occupied by the Vaughan family,
a minor gentry family, from the mid C16th until the latter part of the C18th.
Several memorial inscriptions relating to the family are preserved in the church
and churchyard. In the early C19th the freehold was acquired by the Bute Estate
and the manorial courts for Llandough and Leckwith were held in Great House.
Externally both farmhouse and barn appeared to be of C19th date. Internally,
however, surviving vernacular detail — a blocked stone fireplace stair and
ogee-stopped beams — suggested a C17th date for the house. The ground floor of
the house was surveyed in unusual circumstances in 1974 by H.J.T. Much detail
was then concealed and it was not possible to examine the first floor and roof
trusses. The house remained partially recorded because of problems of access
created by an ownership dispute. The house and farm buildings were suddenly and
completely demolished by B.P. Properties Ltd. on 6th December 1988 amid
The plan of Great House was not published in the Inventory of Farmhouses &
Cottages because of the incompleteness of the available information but it was
classified as a sub-medieval house of direct-entry type. However, certain
features suggested that the core of the house may have been medieval. The
clearly-defined cross-passage end-chimney plan with masonry partitions and
external wall batter (on the unreconstructed N side) had clear affinities with
Brynwell, a medieval farmhouse in the neighbouring parish of Leckwith. Brynwell
was built as a direct-entry, end-chimney, storeyed pre-Reformation house
Brynwell, like Great House, was modernised in the C19th by the Bute Estate but
the medieval date of the house is clearly shown by a small first-floor cusped-head
window and the remodelled roof trusses. Unfortunately it was not possible to
examine the fabric of Great House before the demolition of the house. Examination
of the rubble brought to light no new features except an ogee-stopped beam with
torus, a form of decoration that is not particularly common in Glamorgan
- Report of 'armour' found under the floor of the rear wing at Great House
c.1880 — this seems to be the medieval ironwork found at Llandough now at the
- The carved dressed-stone capital(?) kept by the front door of the house,
presumably from the old church, was lost during the demolition.
- Sherds of C12th, C13th, and early C14th pottery found on steep slope
immediately NE of house, implying occupation of site at that date.
